title: What Equipment Do You Need to Be a YouTuber?
summary: The equipment you actually need for YouTube, from a camera and microphone to lighting, support and editing software.
body_markdown:
So, you're ready to start a YouTube channel. What gear do you actually need?


Less than most shopping lists suggest. Start with equipment that fixes a problem your viewers can notice. A clear voice, steady picture and visible face matter more than a shelf full of accessories.


## The essential YouTube equipment checklist


1. A camera you already know how to use
2. A microphone suited to your recording space
3. One reliable light source
4. A stable mount or tripod
5. Editing software
6. Headphones and storage for checking and protecting your work


You do not need to buy all of it on day one. Make one video, review the result and upgrade the weakest part.


## Camera: start with what you have


A recent phone, webcam or camera can all be a sensible starting point. Before buying another camera, learn to control framing, focus, exposure and the light in front of you.


For screen tutorials, the screen recording is the main picture. A small webcam or phone frame is usually enough for your face. For handheld work, demonstrations or filming at a distance, a dedicated camera may give you more lens and mounting options, but it also adds batteries, memory cards and file transfers to the workflow.


**Buy a camera when:** your current device cannot hold focus, work in your usual light or connect to the lenses and accessories your videos require.


## Microphone: match it to the room


Audio problems distract viewers quickly. Choose the microphone by connection and location rather than by what appears in a podcast studio.


- A **USB microphone** connects directly to a computer and keeps a desk setup simple.
- An **XLR microphone** needs an audio interface or mixer, but gives you a more expandable setup.
- An **on-camera shotgun microphone** is shaped for camera-based filming away from a desk.
- A **wireless or wired lavalier** keeps the microphone close when you need to move.


Current examples include the[RØDE PodMic USB](https://rode.com/en-us/products/podmic-usb) , which offers both USB-C and XLR connections, and the[Shure SM7B](https://www.shure.com/en-US/products/microphones/sm7b) , a dynamic XLR microphone with internal shock isolation and a pop filter. The SM7B needs an interface and supporting gear, so it is not the simplest first purchase.


For more choices, see our guide to the[best microphones for YouTube](https://www.tella.com/blog/best-microphones-for-youtube) .


## Lighting: one soft source is enough to begin


Before buying lights, face a window and record a test. If daylight changes too much or you often film at night, add one controllable light in front of you and slightly to one side.


A diffuser or softbox spreads the source and softens shadows. Keep mixed lighting under control: a daylight window and a warm room lamp can give different parts of the frame different colors.


## Support, power and storage


A stable mount matters more than an elaborate camera move. Use a tripod, desk stand or monitor mount that safely supports the device you own.


Then cover the unglamorous basics:


- Keep spare power or a charger within reach.
- Check that your memory card or computer has enough free space before a long take.
- Use headphones to catch hum, clipping and background noise.
- Back up original recordings before deleting them from the camera or phone.


## Editing and screen recording software


Your editor should match the work you make.[DaVinci Resolve](https://www.blackmagicdesign.com/products/davinciresolve) has a free version that combines editing, color, visual effects and audio tools. It is powerful, but can be more software than a straightforward tutorial needs.


[Tella](https://www.tella.com/) records your screen and camera in the browser, then lets you edit the result, remove pauses and add captions in the same workflow. That keeps the setup lighter for product demos, tutorials and presentations.


## What should you buy first?


Make a test video with your current device, daylight and the quietest room available. Watch it with headphones.


- If the voice is distant or echoey, improve microphone placement or buy a suitable microphone first.
- If the face is dark or grainy, improve the light before replacing the camera.
- If the picture shakes, add a stable mount.
- If production takes too long, simplify the recording and editing workflow.


The best starter kit is the smallest one that lets you publish consistently. Add equipment only when you can name the problem it will solve.
